messages:
Mina Haddad: For incident-bot restricted-mode posting (customer-sensitive incidents) — can we align on the Slack behavior + channel allowlist? We’ve got PM asking for “minimal metadata in #incidents, full bundle somewhere restricted” but I want to make sure we’re not creating a compliance footgun.

Ethan Park: +1. We need a source of truth for “sensitive”. Is that coming from the incident tool (severity + flags) or are we relying on responders to set it manually?

Priya Natarajan: The proposal from SRE side was: incident created => has `visibility = public|restricted`. Default public. Restricted when we know it’s customer-specific (named customer, regulated workload, potential data exposure, etc). Bot reads it from the incident record.

Rafael Mendes: yeah, we can add a field in the incident intake form / template. We also want a manual override command in-thread like `@incident-bot restricted on` for when we realize mid-stream.

Marcus Lin: jumping in w/ security/compliance hat. A couple constraints:
- In any non-restricted channel (#incidents, #eng), bot output must not include customer identifiers (names, tenant IDs), payload snippets, prompt/output samples, or request headers.
- “Minimal metadata” needs to be truly minimal. Even “service + region + time window” is fine, but no “customer X in us-east”.
- Restricted channel must be private, membership controlled, and we should have an auditable list of members (ideally via usergroup) + change history.
- Don’t post links that leak sensitive details via URL params (Grafana links sometimes include query text; same for Kibana/Log links).

Benji Okafor: For channels, are we thinking one global private channel like `#incidents-restricted`? Or per-incident private channels?

Rafael Mendes: per-incident private channels is too much admin overhead IMO. SREs don’t want to manage invites at 3am.

Priya Natarajan: also per-incident private channels breaks the “bot is immediately useful in 2–5 min” goal. People won’t be in the right channel.

Ethan Park: A single `#incidents-restricted` seems simplest. But we need an allowlist so bot doesn’t accidentally post full bundles into random channels.

Mina Haddad: Exactly. What I want is:
1) Bot only posts restricted bundle to a configured set of channel IDs.
2) If restricted mode is on, the bot posts a stub to the public incident thread (so responders know it ran) but no sensitive content.

Marcus Lin: stub message is fine, but be careful with channel mentions. Mentioning `#incidents-restricted` is probably OK (it won’t show content), but don’t include an invite link. Also the stub should not include the customer name or incident title if the title includes customer name.

Benji Okafor: Titles are often “Customer ABC 5xx” :grimacing: so we should assume incident titles are unsafe.

Rafael Mendes: We can standardize that for restricted incidents the public-facing title becomes generic (“Restricted incident - latency regression”) and the detailed title stays in the incident tool / restricted channel.

Priya Natarajan: That’s a process change but probably worth it.

Ethan Park: Implementation-wise, we can do something like:
- `restricted_mode: true` => bot determines `target_channels = restricted_allowlist`
- it posts full bundle only to those channels
- it posts public stub to the incident thread where it was invoked (or where it auto-posts)

Ethan Park: config sketch:
```yaml
incident_bot:
  posting:
    public_channels_allowlist:
      - C02INCIDENTS   # #incidents
    restricted_channels_allowlist:
      - C07RESTRICTED  # #incidents-restricted
    restricted_stub_template: |
      ":lock: Restricted incident context bundle generated. Full details posted to the restricted incident channel."
```

Mina Haddad: Can we make it default-deny? Like if restricted is on and `restricted_channels_allowlist` is empty => bot posts only stub + logs an error.

Ethan Park: yes, that’s the safest.

Marcus Lin: +1 default-deny. Also add audit logging:
- whenever restricted bundle is generated, log event: incident ID, who triggered, which collectors ran, which channels posted to, redaction mode, and a hash of the bundle payload (not the payload itself).
That helps for SOC2 evidence and internal reviews.

Priya Natarajan: Where do we store audit log? existing platform event stream?

Benji Okafor: we can emit to the same “ops events” stream we’re using for deploy/config annotations, but with a different `event_type` (e.g. `incident_bot.restricted_post`).

Rafael Mendes: re: links in restricted bundle — we still want Grafana / trace links for responders. But Marcus’s point is valid: some links embed query text.

Marcus Lin: Ideally we use “safe links”: prebuilt dashboards with variables set via IDs, not raw log queries containing customer identifiers. And if we do include a link to logs, it should be to a saved search template, not a full query string.

Priya Natarajan: For config diffs: even in restricted channel we should still redact secrets / tokens. So “restricted mode” is not “no redaction”, it’s “less restrictive audience”.

Ethan Park: agreed. Restricted mode should still run redaction pipeline. It just changes where we post and what we include by default.

Benji Okafor: Edge case: someone runs `@incident-bot context` in a random channel (not #incidents) during a sensitive incident. We must not post full bundle into that channel.

Ethan Park: That’s where allowlist helps. If invoked from non-allowlisted channel:
- public mode: either refuse or DM the requester with info
- restricted mode: post stub only (or even refuse) + post full bundle to restricted channel

Mina Haddad: What about DMs? Slack DMs are not “audited channel membership” in the same way.

Marcus Lin: please avoid sending restricted incident context via DMs. Harder to control and it persists.

Rafael Mendes: ok. So for now:
- restricted full bundle only goes to `#incidents-restricted`
- no DM behavior
- if invoked elsewhere, bot replies with “can’t post here; see restricted channel / contact oncall-sre” (generic)

Priya Natarajan: Who’s responsible for managing membership in `#incidents-restricted`?

Marcus Lin: Security can own policy. Practically: tie membership to an oncall usergroup (SRE + incident commanders + a few platform leads). Add a quarterly review of membership.

Benji Okafor: We should also ensure `#incidents-restricted` has stricter retention settings if possible.

Marcus Lin: yes. I’ll check with IT on Slack retention controls for private channels (we can’t promise anything yet but we should try).

Ethan Park: Action items I’m hearing:
1) Implement restricted posting mode with default-deny allowlists
2) Add stub behavior for restricted incidents (no customer/title)
3) Emit audit events for restricted posting
4) Use safe links only; avoid embedding sensitive query strings
5) Define process for “restricted incident titles” + membership policy for restricted channel

Rafael Mendes: sounds right. I’ll sync with Sean/Aisha and fold into ENG-2847 scope (posting controls) + ENG-2843 (config diff redaction) so it’s not an afterthought.

Mina Haddad: Great. Ethan can you drop that yaml snippet in the PR when you wire it? I want reviewers to see default-deny clearly.

Ethan Park: will do. I’ll also add tests: restricted incident invoked from non-allowlisted channel => no full bundle posted, only stub + audit event.

Marcus Lin: please @mention me when the PR is up; I want to review before broad rollout.

incident-bot: (auto) Reminder set by Rafael Mendes: "Follow up on restricted-mode allowlist + audit logging" in 2 days.

Priya Natarajan: :thumbsup: also adding note: we should ensure restricted mode is region-aware too (don’t aggregate across regions if it increases risk of exposing wrong customer traffic patterns). Might be Phase 2 but flagging.

Rafael Mendes: good call, will capture.
